specPoints.text: understand the role of yeast in the production of food including bread

primer.text: Yeast is a single-celled fungus with two respiration modes, and bread is its showcase. Enzymes in the yeast release sugars from flour starch, the carbon dioxide from fermentation lifts the dough, and the oven's heat evaporates the ethanol and kills the yeast to finish the loaf.

lessons.title: One Fungus, Two Respirations
lessons.opening: Yeast is a single-celled fungus that switches between aerobic and anaerobic respiration as conditions change. In bread dough it first respires with the available oxygen, then pivots to fermentation once the oxygen runs out, producing the carbon dioxide that matters most to bakers.
keyPoints: Microorganisms are used by humans to produce foods and useful substances.
Yeast is a single-celled fungus capable of aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
Enzymes from the yeast break starch in the flour down into sugars it can respire.
Aerobic respiration runs first, and anaerobic respiration takes over when oxygen runs out.

low.restatement: Yeast is a one-cell fungus that breathes with air first, then ferments when the air is gone.
low.analogy: A swimmer who uses the pool's air at the surface and switches to holding breath underwater.
low.examPointer: State both respiration modes in your definition — naming only anaerobic loses the mark.

medium.restatement: Yeast, a single-celled fungus, begins respiring aerobically in fresh dough and switches to anaerobic respiration once oxygen is exhausted, having first used secreted enzymes to split flour starch into respirable sugars.
medium.analogy: A market trader who sells from a stall (aerobic) until closing time, then moves to home delivery (anaerobic) with the same stock.
medium.examPointer: Credit the enzyme step: starch-to-sugar digestion is a required link between flour and fermentation.

check.stem: What kind of organism is yeast?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Yeast belongs to the fungi.
Yeast cells live singly.
Fungi form their own kingdom.

check.stem: Which two respiration modes can yeast carry out?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Yeast cannot photosynthesise.
The anaerobic mode is essential to bread.
Photosynthesis never occurs in fungi.

check.stem: How does yeast access the energy stored in flour?

options.text: Its enzymes break the starch in flour down into usable sugars
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Starch must be digested to sugars first.

options.text: It dissolves the flour with acid
options.explanation: Enzymes, not acid, do the digesting.

options.text: It burns the flour directly for heat
options.explanation: Respiration is chemical, not burning.

check.stem: When does yeast switch from aerobic to anaerobic respiration in dough?

options.text: When the oxygen trapped in the dough runs out
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Aerobic respiration runs first.
Switching happens long before the oven.
Sugar shortage stops all respiration, not just the aerobic mode.

check.stem: A baker's dough smells faintly alcoholic before baking. What explains that?

options.text: Anaerobic respiration in the yeast produced ethanol as well as carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: The flour was brewed before milling
options.explanation: Flour processing adds no alcohol.

options.text: The yeast photosynthesised sugars into alcohol
options.explanation: Yeast never photosynthesises.

options.text: Water in the dough fermented by itself
options.explanation: Fermentation needs the yeast cells.

check.stem: State what yeast is, in biological terms.
check.modelAnswer: Yeast is a one-cell fungus able to respire both aerobically and anaerobically.

check.stem: Name the molecule in flour that yeast enzymes break down.
check.modelAnswer: Enzymes from the yeast break down starch in the flour into sugars for respiration.

check.stem: Explain why yeast needs both respiration modes during bread making.
check.modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration supports early growth while oxygen lasts, and anaerobic respiration then keeps the cells alive while producing the carbon dioxide that raises the dough.

check.stem: A bakery warms its dough room well but seals every bowl tightly. Predict the respiration pattern.
check.modelAnswer: The yeast will exhaust the trapped oxygen quickly and rely almost entirely on anaerobic respiration, so plenty of carbon dioxide forms but ethanol also accumulates in the sealed bowls.

lessons.title: How Yeast Raises the Loaf
lessons.opening: The rising loaf is gas engineering: carbon dioxide from fermentation collects in small air pockets throughout the dough and puffs up its volume. Baking then evaporates the ethanol, kills the yeast with heat, and fixes the open crumb structure that makes bread bread.
keyPoints: Carbon dioxide released by the yeast collects in small air pockets throughout the dough.
Trapped gas increases the volume of the dough, making it rise.
Baking in a hot oven evaporates the ethanol produced by fermentation.
The oven temperature kills the yeast, ending all further respiration in the loaf.

low.restatement: Bubbles puff the dough up, the oven boils off the alcohol and kills the yeast, and bread comes out.
low.analogy: Inflating a mattress one balloon at a time, then sun-drying it into shape.
low.examPointer: Give both oven effects — ethanol evaporation and yeast death — for the full baking marks.

medium.restatement: Fermenting yeast fills dough air pockets with carbon dioxide so the volume rises; oven heat then evaporates the ethanol and kills the yeast cells, stopping respiration permanently and setting the risen structure.
medium.analogy: A theatre show that ends with the actors (yeast) taking their final bow and the stage lights burning off the fog.
medium.examPointer: If asked why bread contains no alcohol, answer evaporation during baking — a classic one-mark application.

check.stem: What makes bread dough rise during proving?

options.text: Carbon dioxide trapped in small air pockets expands the volume
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Yeast cells dividing to fill space
options.explanation: Rising comes from gas, not cell crowding.
Ethanol is liquid, not the lifting gas.

options.text: Water steaming inside the raw dough
options.explanation: Steam matters in the oven, not during proving.

check.stem: Why does finished bread contain no alcohol?

options.text: The oven heat evaporates the ethanol produced during fermentation
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Anaerobic respiration does produce it.
No absorption claim applies.
No such additive exists in the process.

check.stem: What happens to the yeast cells during baking?

options.text: The high oven temperature kills them, stopping respiration
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: They become dormant and revive later
options.explanation: Bread yeast does not revive.

options.text: They multiply faster in the heat
options.explanation: Heat kills rather than multiplies them.
Cells cannot transform into starch.

check.stem: Which respiration product gives the crumb its open texture?

options.text: Carbon dioxide, held in the air pockets set during baking
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Ethanol leaves as vapour without shaping crumb.
Yeast consumes oxygen; it does not release it.
Water contributes crust, not the taught texture.

check.stem: A baker forgets the yeast entirely. Predict the loaf.

options.text: Dense and flat, because no carbon dioxide forms to raise the dough
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Without yeast no gas is generated.
No fermentation means no ethanol either.

options.text: Rising in the oven by steam
options.explanation: Oven steam cannot replace proving.

check.stem: State the gas that leavens bread dough and its source.
check.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide produced by the yeast during anaerobic respiration leavens the dough.

check.stem: Name the two effects of oven heat on the fermenting dough.
check.modelAnswer: Baking evaporates the ethanol and kills the yeast cells, ending respiration.

check.stem: Explain why killing the yeast in the oven is necessary for the finished loaf.
check.modelAnswer: Dead yeast stops respiration, so the risen shape stays fixed instead of continuing to change, and no further alcohol accumulates in the crumb.

check.stem: A bakery wants a taller loaf. Apply the gas law of proving to suggest one change.
check.modelAnswer: Give the dough a longer or warmer prove so the yeast generates more carbon dioxide, filling more air pockets before baking.

glossary.definition: A single-celled fungus able to respire aerobically and anaerobically.
The flour-and-water mixture that yeast leavens into bread.
The complex carbohydrate in flour that yeast enzymes break down into sugars.
The gas spaces in dough that give baked bread its open texture.
